section.title: The Tenants, the Questions, and the Widow's Mite
section.sectionRationale: In the temple, Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants, exposing the leaders as those who reject the owner's servants and finally his beloved son. A barrage of hostile questions follows, on taxes, resurrection, and the greatest commandment, each turned back with wisdom, until no one dares ask more. Jesus then asks His own question about the Christ as David's Lord, warns against the scribes, and commends a poor widow whose two coins outweigh the rich.
section.thesis: Jesus is the beloved Son and rejected cornerstone whom the tenants kill, the Lord greater than David, who silences every hostile question, sums up the law as love for God and neighbour, and measures true giving not by amount but by the whole-hearted devotion of a poor widow.
section.frameNote: Six beats: the parable of the wicked tenants; the question about taxes to Caesar; the Sadducees on the resurrection; the greatest commandment; the Christ as David's Lord; and the warning about the scribes with the widow's offering.

units.label: The parable of the wicked tenants

verses.text: Then Jesus began to speak to them in parables: “A man planted a {{ampelon|vineyard}}. He put a wall around it, dug a wine vat, and built a watchtower. Then he rented it out to some tenants and went away on a journey.
At harvest time, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect his share of the fruit of the vineyard.
But they seized the servant, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.
Then he sent them another servant, and they struck him over the head and treated him shamefully.
He sent still another, and this one they killed. He sent many others; some they beat and others they killed.
Finally, having one beloved son, he sent him to them. ‘They will respect my son,’ he said.
But the tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’
So they seized the son, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.
What then will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.
Have you never read this Scripture: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the {{gonias|cornerstone}}.
This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?”
At this, the leaders sought to arrest Jesus, for they knew that He had spoken this parable against them. But fearing the crowd, they left Him and went away.

units.label: Paying taxes to Caesar
units.note: give to God what is God's

verses.text: Later, they sent some of the Pharisees and Herodians to catch Jesus in His words.

“Teacher,” they said, “we know that You are honest and seek favor from no one. Indeed, You are impartial and teach the way of God in accordance with the truth. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not? Should we pay them or not?”
But Jesus saw through their hypocrisy and said, “Why are you testing Me? Bring Me a denarius to inspect.”
So they brought it, and He asked them, “Whose image is this? And whose inscription?” “Caesar’s,” they answered.
Then Jesus told them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” And they marveled at Him.

units.label: The Sadducees and the resurrection
units.note: He is not the God of the dead, but of the living

verses.text: Then the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to Jesus and questioned Him:
“Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no children, the man is to marry his brother’s widow and raise up offspring for him.
Now there were seven brothers. The first one married and died, leaving no children.
Then the second one married the widow, but he also died and left no children. And the third did likewise.
In this way, none of the seven left any children. And last of all, the woman died.
In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be? For all seven were married to her.”
Jesus said to them, “Aren’t you mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God?
When the dead rise, they will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven.
But concerning the dead rising, have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses, how God told him, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’?
He is not the God of the dead, but of the living. You are badly mistaken!”
Now one of the scribes had come up and heard their debate. Noticing how well Jesus had answered them, he asked Him, “Which commandment is the most important of all?”
Jesus replied, “This is the most important: ‘Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One.
{{agapao|Love}} the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’
The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ No other commandment is greater than these.”
“Right, Teacher,” the scribe replied. “You have stated correctly that God is One and there is no other but Him,
and to love Him with all your heart and with all your understanding and with all your strength, and to love your neighbor as yourself. This is more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.”
When Jesus saw that the man had answered wisely, He said, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And no one dared to question Him any further.
While Jesus was teaching in the temple courts, He asked, “How can the scribes say that the Christ is the Son of David?
Speaking by the Holy Spirit, David himself declared: ‘The {{kyrios|Lord}} said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.”’
David himself calls Him ‘Lord.’ So how can He be David’s son?” And the large crowd listened to Him with delight.

units.label: The scribes and the widow's offering
units.note: she gave all she had to live on

verses.text: In His teaching Jesus also said, “Watch out for the scribes. They like to walk around in long robes, to receive greetings in the marketplaces,
and to have the chief seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.
They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation.”
As Jesus was sitting opposite the treasury, He watched the crowd putting money into it. And many rich people put in large amounts.
Then one poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which amounted to a small fraction of a denarius.
Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury.
For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.”

ampelon.gloss: A vineyard. In Isaiah 5 the vineyard is Israel, planted and tended by God. Jesus takes up that image: the owner is God, the tenants are Israel's leaders, the servants are the prophets, and the beloved son is Jesus, so the parable is a history of God's patience and Israel's rebellion.

gonias.gloss: The head of the corner, the cornerstone or capstone that holds a structure together. Quoting Psalm 118, Jesus identifies Himself as the stone the builders, the leaders, reject, whom God nonetheless makes the cornerstone of His new building through the resurrection.

agapao.gloss: To love with the whole self, a love of the will and the affections. The greatest commandment is to love God with all one's heart, soul, mind, and strength, and the second, to love one's neighbour as oneself. All the law hangs on this wholehearted love.

kyrios.gloss: Lord, master, the term the Greek Old Testament uses for God's name. In Psalm 110 David calls the Messiah my Lord, so the Christ is not merely David's descendant but David's Lord, greater than David, a hint of the divine dignity of the Son of David.

basic.context: Jesus tells a parable: a man plants a vineyard, rents it to tenants, and sends servants for the fruit, but the tenants beat and kill them, and finally kill the owner's beloved son to seize the inheritance. The owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others. The leaders know it is about them. Then come three trap questions. On taxes, Jesus says give to Caesar what bears Caesar's image, and to God what is God's. To the Sadducees who deny resurrection, He shows from Moses that God is the God of the living. To a sincere scribe, He names the greatest commands: love God wholly and your neighbour as yourself. Then Jesus asks how the Christ can be both David's son and David's Lord. He warns against the showy, greedy scribes, and finally commends a poor widow who gives two tiny coins, all she had, more than all the rich.
basic.hermeneutics: The parable is a compressed history of salvation and a veiled announcement of Jesus' own death and vindication. The three questions show Jesus' wisdom silencing every faction. The greatest commandment gathers the whole law into love. The Christ-as-David's-Lord question presses His true identity. The widow closes the temple scenes with the true measure of devotion: not the size of the gift but the heart behind it.
basic.originalLanguages: The ampelon, vineyard, is Israel; the beloved son is Jesus, the rejected stone made the gonias, cornerstone. The greatest command is to agapao, love, God wholly and neighbour as self. And David, by the Spirit, calls the Christ kyrios, Lord.
basic.typology: The vineyard fulfils Isaiah 5; the rejected cornerstone fulfils Psalm 118. The Son sent last and killed is Jesus. The Christ as David's Lord in Psalm 110 points to His enthronement at God's right hand.
basic.christ: Jesus is the beloved Son sent last and killed, the rejected stone God makes the cornerstone, and the Lord greater than David enthroned at God's right hand. He is the wisdom that silences every challenge.
basic.god: God is the patient owner who sends servant after servant and at last His Son. God is the God of the living, whose power raises the dead. God claims wholehearted love and weighs the heart, not the amount, of every gift.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 5 gives the vineyard song. Psalm 118 and Psalm 110 supply the cornerstone and David's Lord. Deuteronomy 6 and Leviticus 19 give the two great commands.
basic.oneStory: The long story of God's patience with a rebellious people reaches its climax: He sends His beloved Son, whom the tenants kill, but God makes the rejected stone the cornerstone of a new people. The Christ is David's Lord, enthroned at God's right hand, and the true worshippers are not the showy scribes but a poor widow who gives her all, a picture of the whole-hearted love the law requires and the cross supremely displays.

context.literary:
Mark 12 is one continuous scene in the temple courts, running without a change of place from the parable in verse 1 to the widow in verse 44. It grows out of the confrontation of Mark 11:27-33, where the chief priests, scribes and elders asked by what authority Jesus acted, and Jesus refused to answer until they answered about John. The parable is His answer by other means: the authority is the owner's own son. After it comes a clear sequence of challenges. Pharisees with Herodians, then Sadducees, then a scribe each put a question, and then Jesus puts one that nobody can answer. The questioners move from trap, to ridicule, to honest inquiry, which is why the third is told he is not far from the kingdom, verse 34, and why after him no one dares ask more.

The parable is built as an escalation. A servant is beaten, a second is wounded in the head and shamed, a third is killed, then many more, verses 2 to 5. The pace slows at verse 6, 'Finally, having one beloved son,' and the owner's hope is spoken aloud before the tenants' plot is spoken in answer. The story does not end as a story. It ends on Scripture, Psalm 118:22-23, so that the tale of a murdered heir turns toward a rejected stone raised to the corner.

The chapter also closes in a pair. Verses 38 to 40 describe teachers who take widows' houses; verses 41 to 44 show a widow who keeps nothing back. Mark adds no comment of his own and lets the two portraits stand side by side. The bookends, tenants who keep what is not theirs and a woman who withholds nothing, frame the whole question of what it means to give God what is God's.
context.historical:
The setting is the courts of Herod's great temple in the final week before the crucifixion, with Jerusalem packed with Passover pilgrims. The parable draws on a world every hearer knew. Wealthy landowners held estates in Galilee and Judea and let them to tenant farmers for a share of the produce, and quarrels over those rents could turn violent. The details of verse 1, a wall, a pit for the juice, a watchtower, are lifted deliberately from Isaiah 5:1-7, where the vineyard is 'the house of Israel.' Jesus' hearers knew at once who the vineyard was, and the leaders knew who the tenants were, which is why verse 12 says they understood the parable was told against them.

The tax question was dangerous because of the coin and the coalition. Herodians backed the family that ruled on Rome's favour; the Pharisees resented both Herod and Rome. They agree on nothing except Jesus. The tax in view was the poll tax paid with the Roman denarius, the very levy whose introduction under direct Roman rule had sparked the revolt of Judas the Galilean, Acts 5:37. To say 'pay' was to be branded a collaborator; to say 'refuse' was to hand them a charge of sedition.

The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy. They accepted only the Torah as binding and denied resurrection and angels, Acts 23:8. Their puzzle rests on the levirate duty of Deuteronomy 25:5-6, which protected a childless widow and the dead man's name. The scribe stands for a real rabbinic debate over which commandments weighed most. In the treasury scene, the copper coins were the smallest in circulation, and Mark's note that they equal a small fraction of a denarius, using a Latin loan word for the Roman coin, suggests he is writing for readers outside Judea.
context.canonical:
Every strand of the chapter is quoted or echoed across the Bible. The vineyard song of Isaiah 5 is the root of the parable, and the Gospels of Matthew and Luke retell it with small changes. Psalm 118, sung by the crowd at the entry in Mark 11:9-10, returns here as the last line of the parable. The early church seized it at once: Peter says it to the rulers, Acts 4:11, and builds a whole argument on it in 1 Peter 2:4-8, joining it to Isaiah 28:16 and to the stone of stumbling. Paul calls Christ the cornerstone of the household of God, Ephesians 2:20.

The two great commandments become the heart of New Testament ethics. Paul says that love fulfils the law, Romans 13:8-10, and says the whole law is summed up in one word, Galatians 5:14, and James calls the second command the royal law, James 2:8. The scribe's remark that love outweighs burnt offerings joins a prophetic line, 1 Samuel 15:22, Hosea 6:6 and Micah 6:6-8.

Psalm 110:1 is the most quoted Old Testament verse in the New. Peter uses it on Pentecost to prove that God has made the crucified Jesus Lord and Christ, Acts 2:34-36; Paul turns the footstool into the reign that continues until every enemy is put down, 1 Corinthians 15:25; and Hebrews opens with it. Finally, Jesus' answer to the Sadducees from Exodus 3:6 is echoed in Hebrews 11:16, where God is 'not ashamed to be called their God,' and the widow's two coins are matched by Paul's account of the poor Macedonian churches, 2 Corinthians 8:1-2 and 8:12.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wrote for believers who were likely meeting hostility and who had to answer a hard question: if Jesus is the Christ, why did Israel's own leaders put Him to death? This chapter is his answer. The rejection was neither a surprise nor a defeat. Jesus saw it coming, named it in a parable, and set it inside Scripture, so that the death of the beloved son becomes the road to the cornerstone. Mark wants his readers to see that the owner's patience is real, that the judgment on those who seize what is not theirs is real too, and that a new people will receive the fruit.

Mark also wants his hearers to learn how Jesus meets hostile questions. He does not dodge and He does not bluster. Each answer cuts to the root: the coin carries a face and so does every person; the Scriptures and the power of God are what the Sadducees did not know; the law is one whole love. The scribe who agrees is welcomed. The question about David is not a trick but an invitation to wonder who this teacher is.

Finally, the widow is for the church. In a chapter full of power, argument and prestige, Mark ends with someone who has none, and says she did more than anyone. Disciples are meant to measure giving, and devotion, by what it costs the giver and not by what it looks like to onlookers.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The parable is a description of a particular history and a particular set of leaders. It is not a licence to say that the church has replaced the Jewish people, or to blame the Jewish people for the cross. Jesus spoke to Jewish rulers in a Jewish temple, His first followers were Jews, and Paul insists that God has not rejected His people, Romans 11:1. The judgment falls on tenants who abuse their trust, which is a warning to every leader entrusted with God's people, not a charge against an ethnic group.

The commands in the chapter are clearer. 'Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's' is a command, but a short one: it sets two claims side by side and leaves Christians to work out the details of citizenship with the rest of Scripture, such as Romans 13:7. The greatest commandment is a plain command for all. The widow, by contrast, is described and praised, not commanded to be copied to the last coin. Jesus does not tell everyone to give everything at once; He shows what whole-heartedness looks like, and Paul later teaches that the gift is judged by what a person has, 2 Corinthians 8:12.

debates.question: What does 'Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's' mean?

views.label: Two spheres, each with its own claim
views.case: Many read the saying as granting the state a real but limited authority over taxes and public order, while God holds the ultimate claim. Paul and Peter both teach that believers should honour governing authorities, Romans 13:1-7 and 1 Peter 2:13-17, which fits this reading. It is the common view across Reformation traditions.

views.label: The coin bears Caesar's image, but you bear God's
views.case: Others hear a deeper echo. The coin is stamped with an image and so belongs to the one whose image it carries; human beings are made in God's image, Genesis 1:27, so the whole person belongs to God. On this reading the saying does not divide life into equal halves but quietly relativises Caesar, whose claim is small beside the claim of God.

views.label: A deliberate evasion that exposes the question
views.case: A third view stresses that Jesus never says what belongs to Caesar. His questioners had to produce the coin themselves, showing they already used Caesar's money, and the trap was sprung with no answer to seize on. The marvel of verse 17 is that He declined both horns of the dilemma.

debates.bearing: The views are not rivals so much as layers. Jesus grants Caesar a real but smaller claim, His reply turns the question toward God's total claim on persons made in His image, and His wisdom leaves His enemies with nothing to charge Him with. What the text does not do is support either a church that ignores the state or a state that demands what is God's.

debates.question: Is Jesus praising the widow, or lamenting her?

views.label: He praises her as the model of devotion
views.case: The traditional reading takes verses 43 and 44 at face value. He calls His disciples to Him, says she gave more than all, and contrasts surplus with poverty. The point is that God measures a gift by the cost to the giver and the trust it shows, as in 2 Corinthians 8:2 and 8:12.

views.label: He laments a system that takes a widow's last coin
views.case: Others point out that the story comes right after verse 40, where scribes 'defraud widows of their houses.' On this reading Jesus is not holding her up as a pattern to copy but grieving that a temple system, and leaders who devour the vulnerable, let a woman give away her whole living. The disciples are about to be told that this temple will fall, Mark 13:2.

views.label: Both together
views.case: A middle view holds that Mark intends the praise and the sorrow at once. The widow's act is truly wholehearted, and the setting shows how corrupt the institution is that receives it. Nothing in the text forces a choice.

debates.bearing: The text never says Jesus rebuked her, and He plainly honours her whole-hearted trust. But the neighbouring verses forbid reading the story as a fundraising text, or as a call to give to any institution regardless of how it treats the poor. Her gift is praised; the system around it is already under judgment.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 6 calls the son agapetos, 'beloved,' and the word is not ornamental. Mark has already used it twice, at the baptism, 1:11, and at the transfiguration, 9:7, where the Father's voice names Jesus 'My beloved Son.' The Greek Old Testament uses the same adjective for Isaac, 'your son, your only son, whom you love,' Genesis 22:2. A reader who has followed Mark hears that the owner's son in the parable is Jesus, and also hears a father who gives up the one he loves.

When the tenants decide to 'seize' and 'kill' the heir, verse 7, the words recall Joseph's brothers: 'Come now, let us kill him,' Genesis 37:20. The echo may be unplanned, but it sets the scene in a family of stories where a rejected beloved son is later raised.

In the tax question the key verb is apodote, 'give back,' verse 17, not simply 'give.' The idea is repayment of what is owed. The coin's 'image,' eikon, is the very word the Greek Bible uses for humanity made in God's image, Genesis 1:26-27. A coin bears a face; a person bears God's. The word translated 'taxes' in verse 14 is kensos, a Latin loan, so even the vocabulary of the question smells of Rome.

Jesus tells the Sadducees that they are 'mistaken,' planasthe, verses 24 and 27, from the verb of wandering astray. His proof is not an obscure text but 'the passage about the bush,' Exodus 3:6, as rabbis cited by place. The trick is in the tense of the argument: God said 'I am,' not 'I was,' the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

The Shema in verse 29 uses heis, 'one,' for the Hebrew echad of Deuteronomy 6:4, and the sentence can be rendered 'the LORD our God, the LORD is one' or 'the LORD alone.' Where the Hebrew has heart, soul and might, Mark lists four faculties, heart, soul, mind and strength, and the scribe in verse 33 names heart, 'understanding,' synesis, and strength. Hebrew leb already covers thought and will, so the Greek spreads out what the one word already held: the whole person is to love God.

The widow's gift is 'two small copper coins' in verse 42, two lepta, the smallest coin. In verse 44 her 'poverty' translates hysteresis, lack or need, set against the rich who gave out of what 'abounded,' perisseuo. The phrase 'all she had to live on' is literally 'her whole living,' holon ton bion, where bios means a person's livelihood and not just life. Verse 40's 'defraud' is katesthio, 'devour,' the same verb used for devouring a house.

typology.type: The vineyard and its tenants, Isaiah 5:1-7
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah sang of a beloved's vineyard on a fertile hill, with stones cleared, a watchtower built and a winepress cut, and sour grapes in the end. He named the vineyard as Israel. Jesus takes the same furniture and adds the tenants, the leaders charged with caring for it, and the owner's long series of messengers, the prophets. The escalation in Christ is that the owner now sends not another servant but His own son, and the question shifts from why the vines gave bad fruit to what the tenants will do to the heir. The type falls short of a final verdict on Israel: the vineyard is not abandoned, since it is given to others to bear fruit, and Paul later says the branches may be grafted back in, Romans 11:23.

typology.type: The beloved son who is sent last and killed, Genesis 22:2 and 37:20
typology.fulfillment: Isaac, the beloved son laid on the altar, and Joseph, the favoured son whom his brothers meant to kill, both lived stories that pointed ahead. Each was spared at the last moment, Isaac by a ram, Joseph by a caravan, and each was raised to a place of blessing. Jesus is the beloved Son who is not spared: God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The pattern is fulfilled at greater cost, since there was no substitute ram. And the exaltation that follows is not only for the family but for the world, as the cornerstone at the head of a new people.

typology.type: The rejected stone made the cornerstone, Psalm 118:22-23
typology.fulfillment: In the psalm a rejected stone is set at the corner, and in the parable the heir is thrown out of the vineyard and then set up as the stone that determines the whole building. Peter calls Jesus 'a chosen and precious cornerstone,' and the believers are living stones built on Him, 1 Peter 2:4-8. Ephesians 2:20-22 adds that the household rises into a holy temple. The correspondence escalates because the building is no longer a temple of limestone, which Jesus has just said will fall, Mark 13:2, but a people. The type falls short only in one respect: a stone is passive, while Christ is the living stone who rises from the dead.

typology.type: The Lord who sits at God's right hand, Psalm 110:1-4
typology.fulfillment: David wrote of someone he called 'my Lord,' who is invited to sit at God's right hand until His enemies are subdued, and who is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek, Psalm 110:4. Jesus asks how the Christ can be David's son and David's Lord. The resolution is that He is both: descended from David, Romans 1:3, and raised above him, Acts 2:34-36. Hebrews works out the priestly half, that Christ is a priest like Melchizedek whose priesthood cannot end, Hebrews 7:17. The psalm points to a reign that is still unfolding, since Paul says Christ must reign until every enemy is put under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:25.

typology.type: The widow who gives all she has, 1 Kings 17:8-16
typology.fulfillment: Elijah met a widow gathering sticks to make a last meal for herself and her son, and she gave him a small cake first, trusting the word of the LORD. Mark's widow echoes her in her poverty and her trust. In Christ the pattern is fulfilled by the One who 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. Jesus is the giver of everything He had to live on, His own life. The widow is a pattern for disciples, not a type of Christ in the strict sense, and her gift cannot pay for anything. Christ's giving does.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by the parable first. In the long line of messengers, the final one is not another prophet but 'a beloved son,' and the tenants' words, 'This is the heir,' recognise what the leaders refuse to admit. Jesus here tells His enemies, in plain view and on their own ground, that He is not one more servant. The same Son is sent 'last,' which in Mark's wording gathers the whole history of God's dealings with Israel into this single moment, and Hebrews says the same: God spoke through the prophets, 'but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son,' Hebrews 1:1-2.

It leads to Christ by the rejected stone. Jesus does not stop at the murder; He sets the death inside the promise of Psalm 118. He is speaking days before the cross, yet He already speaks of what God will do after it. The thrown-out son is the head of the corner. Peter preached exactly this, Acts 4:10-11, and the early church found in Psalm 118 the pattern of cross and resurrection.

It leads to Christ by His wisdom. In three exchanges He turns the traps on those who set them, and the third silences the room. Colossians says that in Him are 'hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,' Colossians 2:3, and Mark shows it at work.

It leads to Christ by the question about David. Jesus is not denying that the Christ is David's son. He is pressing the deeper point that the Christ is also David's Lord, a figure the psalm presents as seated beside God. The New Testament answers the riddle in the resurrection: Jesus is 'the Root and the Offspring of David,' Revelation 22:16, both David's source and his descendant.

It leads to Christ by the two commandments. The scribe is told he is 'not far from the kingdom,' and that nearness is a person, because the whole law's love is fulfilled in Jesus alone, who loved the Father with every faculty and gave Himself for neighbours and enemies alike, Romans 10:4 and Ephesians 5:2.

Finally the widow points to Him by contrast and by likeness. She gives her whole living; He will give His. Paul sets the Macedonians' poverty beside the Lord's: He who was rich became poor, 2 Corinthians 8:9. A caution keeps the reading honest. The widow is not a hidden symbol of Christ, and the two coins are not a code. The chapter points to Him by what He says and by the way the New Testament quotes it, not by finding Him behind every detail.
study.god:
The parable shows a God of astonishing patience. The owner sends servant after servant, and each is beaten, wounded or killed, and still he sends another. Isaiah's song had the same restraint: 'What more could I have done for My vineyard than I already did for it?' Isaiah 5:4. This patience is not weakness. Paul says God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance, Romans 2:4, and Peter says He is patient, not wishing that any perish, 2 Peter 3:9. Yet patience has an end, and verse 9 is plain that the owner will come. Mercy that is spent on those who will not repent is not endless, and the Bible holds both truths at once.

He is the God who gives His Son. The owner's reasoning in verse 6, 'They will respect my son,' is human hope in a story, but the reality behind it is that the Father sent the Son knowing what would happen. The cross is not an accident the owner failed to foresee. Psalm 118 says of the stone, 'This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes,' so the rejection serves the very purpose God had in view.

He is the living God. Jesus reads Exodus 3:6 as a statement about God's present tense: He is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and 'He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.' The patriarchs are alive to Him, Luke 20:38, and Hebrews says He is not ashamed to be their God because He has prepared a city for them, Hebrews 11:16. The God who made a covenant with them cannot leave them in the grave. That is why the resurrection is not an extra but a consequence of who God is, and why Jesus says the Sadducees know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.

He is the one God who claims the whole person. The Shema declares that the LORD is one, and the one God asks for love with heart, soul, mind and strength. This is not a rival to Caesar's claim but a different order of claim entirely, since only God may ask for all. Jesus also ties love of God and love of neighbour together, so a God who is one is a God whose character shapes how people are treated.

He is the God who weighs hearts. The scribe says love matters more than offerings, and Jesus approves; the widow's two coins outweigh the larger gifts. God sees what is given and what is kept back, 1 Samuel 16:7.

He speaks as Trinity without announcing it. David speaks 'by the Holy Spirit,' verse 36; the LORD speaks to David's Lord; the owner sends the Son. For worship this means that we come to a God who is one yet has shown Himself as Father, Son and Spirit, who is patient yet will judge, who gives everything and so can rightly ask for everything.

crossReferences.note: The song behind the parable. Isaiah's vineyard has the same wall, watchtower and winepress, and the same disappointed owner. Where Isaiah says the vineyard itself bore sour fruit, Jesus shifts the blame to the tenants who run it, and adds the son. Reading the two together shows how Jesus reshapes an old text to name the leaders and announce the Son.

The rejected stone that closes the parable. The same psalm supplied the crowd's welcome in Mark 11:9-10, so the one who is greeted as the coming one is also the one who is thrown out and then made the cornerstone. It joins palm branches and cross in one song.

Joseph's brothers see him coming and plot to kill him, 'Come now, let us kill him.' The tenants' plan in Mark 12:7 echoes the wording. In both stories the beloved son is thrown out, and in Joseph's story God turns the evil into the salvation of many, Genesis 50:20.

The levirate law the Sadducees twist into a riddle. It was meant to protect a widow and a dead man's name. They treat it as a puzzle about the afterlife, when it was a law about care for the vulnerable, and Jesus lifts the discussion from the puzzle to the God who raises the dead.

Jesus' proof that the dead live. At the bush God introduces Himself to Moses as the God of the fathers, and the present tense holds them in His keeping. The Sadducees accepted only Moses, so Jesus argues from the very books they honoured.

The Shema, the creed Israel recited morning and evening. Jesus quotes it whole, beginning with the confession that the LORD is one. The command to love comes from the oneness: because God is one, He can be loved with an undivided heart.

The second commandment comes from the same chapter that forbids revenge and grudges against fellow Israelites. Jesus joins this humble line to the Shema and says no commandment is greater than the pair. Love of neighbour is not an extra duty but the same love turned outward.

The text Jesus uses to press the question of the Christ. It is the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most often, and the picture of the Son seated at God's right hand returns at the trial in Mark 14:62.

Peter, before the same Sanhedrin that rejected Jesus, quotes the cornerstone psalm and says that the stone the builders rejected is the crucified and risen Jesus. The parable has become a sermon, and it shows that the early church understood Psalm 118 as the key to the cross.

Peter joins Psalm 118 to Isaiah 28:16 and calls Jesus the living stone, precious to those who believe and a stumbling stone to those who do not. He then turns believers into living stones, a spiritual house. The parable's new tenants are the people built on the cornerstone.

Paul's counsel on taxes: pay what is owed, taxes to those owed taxes, respect to those owed respect. This is the apostolic echo of 'Give to Caesar what is Caesar's.' It keeps the saying from being read as a call to avoid the state.

The widow of Zarephath has only a handful of flour and a little oil, yet obeys the prophet's word and finds the jar unfailing. A widow's whole supply given in trust is a pattern older than the temple widow, and the two stories suggest that God honours what He is given in faith.

Paul tells the Corinthians of Macedonian believers whose 'deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity.' It is the widow's story told of a whole community, and Paul's judgment in verse 12, that a gift is measured by what one has, is Jesus' verdict in Mark in other words.

Jesus calls Himself 'the Root and the Offspring of David.' The riddle of Mark 12:35-37, how David's son can be David's Lord, is answered in one verse: He is the origin of David and his descendant, the Lord who became the son.

study.oneStory:
The chapter picks up the Bible's story at several points at once. At creation, God made people in His image, and the coin question quietly recalls that: a coin belongs to the one whose face is on it, and a person belongs to the one whose image he bears, Genesis 1:27. At the fall, humanity grasped what was not its own, and the tenants repeat Adam's grasp: they want the inheritance without the owner. The whole Old Testament is the owner's patient search for fruit among those who hold His vineyard, through patriarchs, judges, kings and prophets, and the messengers keep arriving.

Redemption arrives in the Son who is sent last. He is thrown out and killed, and then, in the same Psalm, made the cornerstone. The chapter therefore stands very near the centre of the story. The questions that follow show the old order's final inability to grasp what is happening: a tax system under Caesar, a theology without resurrection, a law without love, a messianic hope without a Lord.

What the chapter sets up is large. The resurrection that the Sadducees denied comes in the next days; the stone becomes the cornerstone of a new temple, the church, Ephesians 2:20-22; the Christ is seated at God's right hand as Lord, Acts 2:34-36; and the one who gave His whole living for many opens the way to the kingdom that the scribe was not far from.

It ends in the new creation. Paul says Christ must reign until every enemy is under His feet, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death, 1 Corinthians 15:25-26. Jesus told the Sadducees that those who rise are like the angels, and Revelation shows the picture: no more death, mourning or pain, Revelation 21:4. There is no temple in the final city, because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22, so the vineyard's long story ends not in a building but in a presence. Those who loved the Lord with all heart, soul, mind and strength will be loved without limit, and the people who gave their whole living in trust, like the widow, will find that they gave to the One who gives everything back.

quiz.q: Who are the characters in the parable of the wicked tenants?

options.text: God the owner, Israel's leaders the tenants, the prophets the servants, and Jesus the beloved son.
options.note: The parable draws on Isaiah 5 and casts Jesus as the son whom the tenants kill.

options.text: A landowner and some dishonest farm workers, with no deeper meaning.
options.note: The leaders knew it was spoken against them; it is a pointed allegory of salvation history.

options.text: God and His rebellious people who reject His messengers and His Son.
options.note: True in outline, but it should specify the leaders as the tenants and Jesus as the beloved son.

options.text: The Romans as tenants oppressing Israel the vineyard.
options.note: The tenants are Israel's own leaders, not Rome; the parable indicts them.

quiz.q: What did Jesus mean by give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's?

options.text: Civil authorities may be given their due, but human beings bear God's image and owe their whole selves to God, who is supreme.
options.note: Mark 12:17; the coin bears Caesar's image, but we bear God's, so God's claim is total.

options.text: That taxes should always be paid without question.
options.note: Jesus affirms limited civic duty, but the weight falls on giving our whole selves to God.

options.text: That earthly rulers have a proper claim while God's claim over us is ultimate.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should include that we bear God's image and owe Him our whole selves.

options.text: That God and Caesar have equal claims on us.
options.note: God's claim is supreme; Caesar's is limited and subordinate.

quiz.q: How did Jesus answer the Sadducees who denied the resurrection?

options.text: God told Moses He is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and He is God of the living, so the dead will rise.
options.note: Mark 12:26-27; the covenant with the patriarchs implies their ongoing life.

options.text: He said they simply needed more faith.
options.note: He said they knew neither the Scriptures nor the power of God, and reasoned from Moses, not merely from faith.

options.text: He showed from Scripture and God's power that they were mistaken.
options.note: True, but it should name the specific proof from the burning bush and the God of the living.

options.text: He agreed marriage continues unchanged in the resurrection.
options.note: Jesus said the risen neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels.

quiz.q: What did Jesus name as the greatest commandments?

options.text: To love God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength, and to love your neighbor as yourself.
options.note: Mark 12:29-31 joins the Shema with Leviticus 19:18.

options.text: To love God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength.
options.note: That is the first and greatest, but Jesus paired it with loving your neighbour as yourself.

options.text: To offer burnt offerings and sacrifices faithfully.
options.note: The scribe rightly noted love is more important than all offerings and sacrifices.

options.text: To keep the Sabbath above all other commands.
options.note: Jesus named love for God and neighbour as the greatest, not the Sabbath specifically.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus commend the poor widow's two small coins?

options.text: Because she gave out of her poverty all she had to live on, unlike the rich who gave from their surplus.
options.note: Mark 12:43-44; her gift was total devotion, measured by the heart, not the amount.

options.text: Because her gift was the largest sum given that day.
options.note: It was the smallest sum, yet the greatest gift, because it was everything she had.

options.text: Because she gave sacrificially rather than from what she could spare.
options.note: Correct in substance, but it should contrast her total giving with the rich giving from surplus.

options.text: Because she gave more cheerfully than the others.
options.note: The text stresses that she gave all she had, not merely that she gave cheerfully.

questions: The tenants wanted the vineyard's fruit without the owner. Where are you tempted to enjoy God's gifts while resisting His claim on your life?
Jesus said we bear God's image and owe Him our whole selves. What would it look like to give God what is God's in a specific area you have held back?
The greatest command is to love God with everything. Which part, heart, soul, mind, or strength, do you most need to bring fully into your love for God?
The scribes loved recognition and long public prayers for show. Where might you be tempted to practice religion for the eyes of others?
The widow gave all she had to live on. What would whole-hearted, trusting generosity look like for you, beyond giving only from your surplus?

translationNotes.note: The cornerstone, literally the head of the corner, renders Psalm 118:22; whether a foundation stone or a capstone, it is the decisive stone the builders discarded and God exalted, applied to Christ.
The LORD said to my Lord quotes Psalm 110:1; the first Lord is God, the second the Messiah, so David, by the Spirit, calls his descendant his Lord, pointing to the Christ's greater dignity.
Two small copper coins renders two lepta, the smallest coins in use, together a tiny fraction of a day's wage; the point is that she gave everything she had.
